about.title: Williams Slip & Fall and Premises Liability Claims
about.longDescription: Williams is a small city, but its mix of highway travelers passing through on I-5 and Rt 20 and local residents shopping along E Street and 8th Street means property owners see steady foot traffic year-round. When a spill, broken step, uneven pavement, or poor lighting isn't addressed, someone gets hurt. Under California law, you generally have to show the property owner or manager knew, or reasonably should have known, about the hazard and didn't fix it or warn you. That's why documenting the scene matters so much here — photos of the hazard, witness names, and any store or gas station surveillance video before it's deleted. Our team evaluates fall claims, gathers evidence, and explains your options. We work on contingency — there's no fee unless we recover compensation for you.

whyChoose.title: What Matters in a Williams Premises Liability Case

items.title: Proving the Owner Had Notice
items.desc: California requires showing the property owner knew or should have known about the hazard and failed to act. We can help pull maintenance logs and inspection records to establish that timeline.

items.title: Preserving Video Before It's Overwritten
items.desc: Many businesses along E Street, 8th Street, and near the I-5 interchange run surveillance systems that overwrite footage within days or weeks. Getting a preservation request out quickly can be the difference in a fall case.

items.title: Understanding Comparative Fault
items.desc: California uses pure comparative fault, so even if you're found partly responsible for the fall, you may still recover a reduced amount. We can help present the facts in a way that reflects the full picture, not just the owner's version.

items.question: I fell at a store off Rt 20 in Williams — what should I do first?
items.answer: If you're able, take photos of exactly what caused the fall, get names of any witnesses, and ask the manager to note the incident in writing. Seek medical attention even if you feel okay at first, since some injuries show up later. From there, we can help you preserve any surveillance footage before it's gone.

items.question: How long do I have to file a slip-and-fall claim in California?
items.answer: Generally you have two years from the date of the fall, but claims against a public entity — like a city-owned sidewalk or county building — carry a much shorter deadline, often just months. It's worth having an attorney review the details early so you don't lose the chance to file.

items.question: Will it hurt my case if I was partly at fault for not seeing the hazard?
items.answer: Not necessarily. California's pure comparative fault rule means you can still recover compensation even if you share some blame, though the amount may be reduced by your percentage of fault. We can help evaluate how strong your notice evidence is and what a fair claim looks like.
